opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really important question, and the honest answer is that the two are quite complementary, so it's hard to cleanly separate their contributions.

Pre-training compute builds up the underlying capabilities: the model's knowledge, its ability to reason, its grasp of language and code. Fine-tuning, whether instruction tuning or reinforcement learning from human feedback, mostly elicits and shapes those capabilities so they show up in a form people find useful. A raw pre-trained model might know a lot, but it doesn't reliably follow instructions or stay on task. Fine-tuning closes that gap.

One way we've tried to think about it is in terms of "compute-equivalent gains." You ask: how much extra pre-training compute would you need to get the same improvement on some benchmark or user-facing task that a given post-training technique gives you? When you look at it that way, a lot of these post-training enhancements look very cost-effective. Things like instruction tuning, better prompting, chain-of-thought, and tool use can give improvements that would correspond to scaling up pre-training by something like several-fold, sometimes more, while costing only a tiny fraction of the original training budget.

So in terms of getting models to do what users actually want, fine-tuning punches well above its weight per unit of compute. But I'd caution against concluding that it substitutes for scale. These techniques tend to work better on more capable base models. RLHF on a small model doesn't get you GPT-4-level behavior; it gets you a nicer-to-use small model. Scale sets the ceiling, and fine-tuning determines how close to that ceiling you actually get in practice.

There's also a trend worth noting: post-training has been getting a larger share of total compute, especially with reinforcement learning on reasoning tasks. So the line between "scaling" and "fine-tuning" is blurring. Increasingly, scaling is happening in the post-training phase and at inference time too, not just in pre-training. From a forecasting perspective, I think that means we shouldn't treat pre-training compute as the only driver, but it's still the foundation that everything else builds on.

r001.rationale: The response says fine-tuning is cost-effective and shapes capabilities into useful behavior, but also calls it complementary to scaling and says scale sets the ceiling. It does not clearly state that fine-tuning contributes more than compute scaling to the desired behaviors.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've looked at fairly carefully at Epoch, and I think the honest answer is that fine-tuning is a surprisingly large part of the story, but it's a different kind of contribution than compute scaling, and it's worth being precise about the distinction.

If you look at the compute side, you have these very regular trends. Training compute for frontier models has been growing something like four to five times per year, and that buys you capabilities in a fairly predictable way through scaling laws. More compute, more data, lower loss, better performance on a broad range of tasks. That's the engine that produces the underlying capability.

But what fine-tuning does, and I'd include things like instruction tuning and RLHF in this, is it unlocks capabilities that are already latent in the base model. The base model, after pretraining, is essentially a very good predictor of internet text. It can do a lot of things, but it doesn't reliably do what you ask, because predicting the next token of a random web document isn't the same objective as being helpful. So fine-tuning is in some sense steering, rather than adding raw capability.

The striking thing, though, is how much that steering is worth when you try to quantify it. One way we've tried to do this is to ask: how much more pretraining compute would you need to get the same benchmark performance without the fine-tuning step? And for some of these post-training techniques, the compute-equivalent gain is quite large. We've seen estimates where things like instruction tuning or chain-of-thought prompting are equivalent to something like a five to twenty-fold increase in training compute, sometimes more, depending on the task. And what makes that remarkable is that the fine-tuning itself typically uses a tiny fraction of the pretraining compute, often well under one percent.

So in terms of cost efficiency, fine-tuning is extraordinarily good value. And I think that's a big part of why the gap between what these models could do in principle and what they do in practice closed so quickly around the time of ChatGPT. The pretraining had been done, the capability was there, and a relatively cheap post-training step made it usable.

That said, I'd offer two caveats. The first is that I don't think fine-tuning can substitute for scaling indefinitely. There's a sense in which it's a one-time dividend. You get a big jump when you first align the model with what users want, but you can't keep extracting another ten-fold compute-equivalent gain by fine-tuning harder. The ceiling is set by what the base model actually knows, and raising that ceiling still comes back to compute and data.

The second caveat is that these two things interact. Fine-tuning seems to work better on larger models. Bigger base models are more steerable, they generalize better from fewer examples, and the alignment transfers more cleanly to tasks you didn't explicitly train on. So it's not really fine-tuning versus scaling. Scaling makes fine-tuning more effective, and fine-tuning makes the scaled model actually worth having.

So if you ask me to split the credit, I'd say the long-run trend in what models can do is overwhelmingly driven by compute and the algorithmic progress that makes compute go further. But the question of whether models do what users want, which is really a question about elicitation and alignment, has been disproportionately shaped by relatively cheap post-training. And I think that's an important point for forecasting, because it means there can be quite abrupt shifts in usable capability that aren't visible if you're only tracking the compute curve.

r001.rationale: The response says that whether models do what users want has been “disproportionately shaped” by relatively cheap post-training, while compute scaling mainly drives underlying capability.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between a model having a capability and being willing or able to deploy it in the way a user wants. Scaling compute has been a major driver of the underlying capabilities. But simply training a larger model to predict text doesn’t necessarily give you a useful assistant. It might continue your question, rather than answer it.

Fine-tuning can make a substantial difference there. With a relatively small amount of additional training, you can get the model to follow instructions, give answers in a useful format, and better reflect user preferences. So its contribution to usefulness can be much larger than its share of the total training compute would suggest.

But I wouldn’t treat those as independent contributions that we can neatly assign percentages to. Fine-tuning draws on capabilities acquired during pretraining, and scaling makes more capabilities available to draw on. They’re complementary. And getting a model to produce responses that users prefer is also a narrower achievement than ensuring it reliably does what they actually intend.

r001.rationale: The response says fine-tuning can substantially improve usefulness and that its contribution is large relative to its compute cost. It does not state that fine-tuning contributes more than compute scaling to the specific behaviors users want; it describes them as complementary.

sol-6.1.text:
I think fine-tuning is quite important for getting models to do what users want, but it plays a different role from scaling. Pretraining gives you a broad set of capabilities, and fine-tuning helps turn those capabilities into behavior that’s useful to a user: following instructions, answering questions directly, and responding in the format you intended.

So you can spend a relatively small fraction of the total compute on fine-tuning and get a very large improvement in how useful the model feels. But I wouldn’t infer from that that fine-tuning is responsible for most of its underlying capabilities. A lot of the work has already been done during pretraining.

The two are complementary. Scaling produces a more capable starting point, and fine-tuning makes it easier to elicit and direct those capabilities. How much credit you assign to each depends on whether you’re measuring underlying capability or how well the system serves a user in practice.

r001.rationale: The response says fine-tuning can greatly improve user-facing usefulness, but describes it as complementary to scaling and does not state that fine-tuning contributes more than scaling to the requested behaviors.
